from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["A circle's area is pi times radius squared.", "A sphere is points equidistant from center.", "Parallel projection creates a flat shadow."]

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        circle = Circle(radius=1.0, color="#FF5733")

        radius_line = Line(circle.get_center(), circle.get_right(), color=WHITE)
        radius_label = MathTex("r", color=WHITE).next_to(radius_line, UP, buff=0.1)
        area_formula = MathTex("A = \\pi r^2", color="#33FF57")

outline.topic: The Geometry of Light: Sphere Surface Area and Its Projected Shadow
outline.target_audience: High school geometry or physics students

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Geometry of Circles and Spheres
sections.content: Briefly review the area of a circle (A = πr²) and define a sphere as a set of points equidistant from a center. Introduce the concept of a 'parallel projection' (orthographic projection) where rays of light are perpendicular to the projection plane.
sections.example: Visualizing a ball casting a circular shadow on the floor when the sun is directly overhead.

sections.title: The Sphere Surface Area Formula
sections.content: Introduce the formula for the surface area of a sphere: S = 4πr². Use a visual animation where the sphere’s surface is 'unrolled' or mapped onto four flat circles of the same radius to demonstrate the coefficient '4'.
sections.example: An orange being peeled and its skin used to perfectly cover the surface area of four flat circular paper discs of the same radius.

sections.title: The Relationship: Sphere Area vs. Projected Shadow
sections.content: Compare the total surface area (4πr²) to the area of the shadow cast on a flat surface (πr²). Highlight that the shadow is exactly 1/4th of the total surface area of the sphere, regardless of the direction of the light source (due to spherical symmetry).
sections.example: A spherical robot hovering in space; if it blocks a laser beam, the 'damage' (shadow area) is always 1/4 of its total metallic surface.

sections.title: Real-World Application & Summary
sections.content: Apply the logic to real-world scenarios. Explain why knowing this 4:1 ratio is critical for calculating heat absorption in space satellites or sunlight exposure for planetary models.
sections.example: A space-faring cat astronaut monitors a spherical oxygen tank; calculating how much of its surface is exposed to intense solar radiation versus its cross-sectional shadow area.
